newsitem.title: USA: Dole says brace for recession if Clinton re-elected.
newsitem.headline: Dole says brace for recession if Clinton re-elected.

text.p: Republican Bob Dole opened the final lap of his campaign on Wednesday with a prayer at the famed Lincoln Memorial and a blistering charge that President Bill Clinton's reelection could lead to a recession.

Dole opened his day in Washington with a short visit to the Lincoln Memorial in Washington dedicated to Republican hero Abraham Lincoln for what he said was inspiration and a moment of silent prayer for the election just six days away.

Way behind in polls, Dole then flew to this small college town near the Kentucky border to hit Clinton on what has been a Clinton strong point, a steadily growing economy, low inflation, a booming stock market and low unemployment.
Dole said Clinton's policies, including a 1993 tax increase, would put the economy into a deep slide.

"It doesn't take a team of economists to tell you what happens when you mix slow growth with tax hikes -- that's a recipe for economic collapse," said Dole in his prepared remarks. "Well, if he is re-elected, brace yourself for the Clinton recession."

In actually delivering the speech, he said the Clinton policy is a "recipe for economic collapse" but veered some from his prepared text to follow with "if this is a recovery, I can hardly wait for the recession."

Dole, whose campaign centred on an economic package and 15 percent income tax cut he said would produce a 3.5 percent economic growth rate, seized on Wednesday's government figures showing a 2.2 percent increase in the gross domestic product for the three months ending September 30.
"This is a real economic slowdown," Dole said, noting it had dropped from the second quarter growth rate.

"And it is disastrous news for American workers and businesses and even worse news for low and middle income Americans who haved been squeezed by lower wages and higher taxes," said Dole to a rally at Austin Peay State University.
He listed other signs he saw of a weak economy and said "so today, all the false, empty talk about the so-called Clinton recovery comes to an end."
"Today the White House should finally wake up and admit that its policy of higher taxes and bigger government has been dragging our economy down," said Dole.
Dole claimed "my economic plan is designed to steer the economic ship the other way."
Dole was introduced by his wife, Elizabeth, who said Dole should be elected because "he is a better man for America."

The Dole stop to the Lincoln Memorial where Dole and Mrs. Dole walked halfway up the steps took his staff by surprise as he so often has done during this campaign. Only a few tourists and a television pool camera recorded the scene, an aide said.
Dole mentioned the stop at the monument to an enthusiastic crowd in Kentucky, telling them he went there for inspiration and a silent prayer.
He was inspired to tell the crowd, "We are going to win this election."
"We can't afford four more years of scandal and weak leadership," Dole said.
"He stopped by the Lincoln memorial for a moment of reflection and good luck on the final sprint to victory," said press secretary Nelson Warfield said earlier.
Dole planned only two speaking events during the day, one in Kentucky and the other in New Orleans before heading to Tampa, Fla., for an overnight stay.
A top Dole political adviser, Charles Black, said Tennessee was a state that Dole could win although he was trailing Clinton, according to the Dole campaign's internal polls.

"We're still a few points down,' Black told reporters."But it's doable. Howard Baker thinks we can win. Lamar thinks we can win if we do our job," mentioning the former Tennessee senator and former Dole opponent and ex-Tennessee governor Lamar Alexander.

Nationally the latest Reuters/Zogby three-day tracking poll showed Dole nearly 10 points behind Clinton, 43.1 to 33.3 percent with Reform Party candidate Ross Perot trailing at 8.1 percent. Clinton lost ground overnight and the movement away from him by 2.4 percentage points appeared to shift into the undecided ranks which numbered 13.1 percent.
